declarations.name: Lemma 1. Terminal mass detects exactly the removable locus
declarations.scope: For every polynomial DT tree on N=2r+1 sheets, lambda(A) is the sum of its two terminal-component sizes minus two. The minimum mu over all factors lies in [0,N-4] and is zero exactly when a DT has two exclusive leaves on different edges.

declarations.name: Lemma 2. Bringing another factor preserves a chosen cut
declarations.scope: For arbitrary factors A,B, move B unchanged toward A, using positive moves from the right or negative moves from the left. All three component sets after deleting A stay literal and connected; both selected factors are unchanged. The cost is their positional distance minus one.

declarations.name: Lemma 3. An outer one-contact gives strict descent
declarations.scope: If mu>0 and a minimizing DT A has support intersection exactly one with B at an outer endpoint a, cut-preserving bringing followed by conjugating B by A strictly reduces mu in at most r-1 ordinary moves. Stop at the first decrease to keep all preceding masses equal. The terminal mass drops by the size of the nonempty branch pruned from the a-component.

declarations.name: Lemma 4. Two degree-two contacts can create two new leaves
declarations.scope: For adjacent A=(ab)(cd),B=(ae)(cf) on six distinct labels, with every other factor fixing a,c, one inverse move produces ((be)(df),A). The two degree-two contacts become exclusive leaves of A; deleting them and A leaves a full-cycle polynomial tuple. Reverse the adjacent input order and use a positive move for the same retained A. No claim about arbitrary bringing preserving these degree conditions.

declarations.name: Lemma 5. Five weighted components control every adjacent-pair rotation
declarations.scope: For any adjacent DT pair, delete its four edges and record five positive component weights and the component of each support label. Every pair rotation has exactly the terminal masses computed on that weighted quotient tree. Q^k(A,B)=(A(AB)^k,A(AB)^(k+1)) and ord(AB) is in {2,3,4,5,6}. An endpoint mass inequality does not control intermediate masses or guarantee any descending pair exists.
